Spider Pest Control: Identification, Risks & Treatment

By Shaw's Pest Control  ·  Wichita, KS

Spider Pest Control: When to Worry and When to Call a Professional

If you're seeing spiders in your home more frequently than usual, you're probably wondering whether you're dealing with a harmless nuisance or something that requires professional spider pest control. The answer depends largely on the species you're encountering, where they're appearing, and what's attracting them in the first place. Here in Wichita and across Kansas, we share our space with several spider species—including two venomous varieties that homeowners should take seriously. Shaw's Pest Control has been helping Kansas families identify and manage spider problems since 1987, and we've learned that effective spider control starts with understanding what you're up against. This guide covers the spiders you're most likely to encounter, how to identify the dangerous ones, and when it's time to bring in professional help.

The Two Venomous Spiders Kansas Homeowners Need to Know

Kansas is home to two medically significant spiders: the brown recluse and the black widow. Both are common throughout the state, and both can cause serious health problems if you're bitten.

Brown recluse spiders are small—about the size of a quarter with legs extended—and tan to dark brown in color. Their most distinctive feature is a dark violin-shaped marking on their back, which is why they're sometimes called "fiddle-back" spiders. They prefer dark, undisturbed spaces like closets, attics, basements, and storage boxes. These spiders are not aggressive, but they will bite if they feel trapped against your skin—often when you're putting on clothing or shoes where they've taken shelter. Brown recluse bites can cause tissue necrosis (skin death) in severe cases, though most bites result in localized pain and a slow-healing wound.

Black widow spiders are easier to identify thanks to their shiny black bodies and distinctive red hourglass marking on the underside of their abdomen. Females are larger and more dangerous than males. They build irregular, tangled webs in protected outdoor areas like woodpiles, sheds, garages, and under deck furniture. Black widow venom is neurotoxic and can cause severe muscle pain, cramping, nausea, and difficulty breathing. Bites require immediate medical attention, especially for children, elderly individuals, or those with compromised immune systems.

If you're seeing either of these species in or around your home, professional spider control in Wichita can eliminate the infestation and reduce the conditions that attract them.

Why You're Seeing More Spiders—and What It Means

Spiders don't invade your home randomly. They follow food sources, which means if you have spiders, you likely have other pests they're feeding on. This is one of the most important things homeowners miss when dealing with spider problems: spiders are secondary pests.

Common prey for indoor spiders includes flies, mosquitoes, ants, moths, and other small insects. If you're noticing an increase in web-building activity or spotting multiple spiders in different areas of your home, it's a signal that you may have an underlying pest problem. Addressing spiders alone won't solve the issue long-term—you need to eliminate their food supply.

Professional pest control for spiders takes a comprehensive approach. It's not just about killing the spiders you see; it's about treating the insects that attract them, sealing entry points, and reducing harborage areas both inside and outside your home. At Shaw's Pest Control, our technicians hold Three State Certifications and Master Tech Certification, which means we're trained to identify the root causes of spider activity and design treatment plans that address the full scope of the problem.

Seasonal patterns also play a role. In Kansas, spider activity peaks in late summer and early fall as temperatures drop and spiders seek shelter indoors. Male spiders become more active during mating season, which is why you might see them wandering across floors or walls. Knowing these patterns helps homeowners distinguish between a temporary uptick in activity and a true infestation.

What Professional Spider Pest Control Actually Involves

Effective spider control isn't about spraying pesticide in every corner and calling it done. It's a targeted, multi-step process that combines treatment, exclusion, and environmental modification.

A thorough inspection comes first. Technicians identify the species present, locate webs and egg sacs, and assess the conditions contributing to the infestation. This includes checking common harborage sites like window wells, crawl spaces, attics, basements, and garage areas. Outdoor inspection focuses on foundation cracks, vents, utility penetrations, landscaping, and areas where moisture or clutter creates ideal spider habitat.

Treatment typically includes interior spot treatments in areas where spiders are active, web removal, and application of residual products in cracks, crevices, and along baseboards. Exterior treatment creates a barrier around the foundation, entry points, eaves, and other vulnerable areas. For brown recluse infestations, dust formulations may be used in voids and attics where spiders hide during the day.

Exclusion work—sealing gaps, repairing screens, and closing off entry points—is just as important as chemical treatment. Spiders can squeeze through openings as small as a credit card, so even minor gaps around doors, windows, and utility lines can invite them inside.

Homeowners in areas like Andover and throughout the Wichita metro often ask whether ongoing service is necessary. For homes with recurring spider problems or those located near wooded areas, fields, or water sources, quarterly treatments provide the best long-term results. These visits maintain a protective barrier, address seasonal pest pressures, and catch new issues before they become infestations.

Spider Control in Wichita: What Local Homeowners Should Expect

Wichita's mix of urban and semi-rural environments creates ideal conditions for both brown recluse and black widow spiders. Homes near open fields, wooded lots, or the Arkansas River corridor tend to see higher spider activity, especially in late summer. Older homes with basements, crawl spaces, or stone foundations are particularly vulnerable to brown recluse infestations.

Local pest control isn't one-size-fits-all. A ranch-style home in west Wichita will have different vulnerabilities than a two-story home with a full basement in Andover. That's why working with a locally owned company matters—we understand the construction styles, common pest pressures, and seasonal patterns specific to south-central Kansas. Shaw's Pest Control has served this area for over 35 years, and that experience shows in how we assess properties and customize treatment plans.

Frequently Asked Questions

What kills spiders instantly?

Direct contact sprays containing pyrethroids or other fast-acting insecticides will kill spiders on contact. However, these products don't provide residual protection or address the underlying pest problem attracting spiders. For lasting spider pest control, you need treatments that create a barrier, eliminate food sources, and prevent re-infestation.

How do I keep spiders out of my house permanently?

Permanent spider control requires a combination of exclusion, sanitation, and ongoing pest management. Seal cracks and gaps around doors, windows, and the foundation. Remove clutter in basements, garages, and storage areas. Reduce outdoor lighting that attracts insects spiders feed on. Schedule regular pest control service to maintain a protective barrier and treat insects before spiders arrive.

Are brown recluse spiders common in Kansas?

Yes, brown recluse spiders are very common throughout Kansas, including the Wichita area. They thrive in undisturbed spaces and are frequently found in homes, especially in basements, closets, attics, and storage areas. Because their bites can cause serious medical issues, professional identification and treatment are recommended if you suspect an infestation.

What attracts spiders to your house?

Spiders are attracted to homes that provide food, shelter, and moisture. The primary attractant is other insects—flies, ants, moths, and small bugs that spiders hunt. Clutter, cardboard boxes, undisturbed storage areas, and dark spaces also create ideal habitat. Cracks in the foundation, gaps around windows and doors, and outdoor vegetation close to the house provide easy entry points.

Can pest control get rid of spiders?

Yes, professional pest control is highly effective at eliminating spider infestations and preventing their return. Treatment includes removing webs and egg sacs, applying residual insecticides to harborage areas and entry points, treating the insects spiders feed on, and sealing gaps that allow access. Ongoing service provides the best long-term protection, especially for homes prone to recurring spider problems.

How long does spider pest control last?

Most professional spider treatments provide protection for 60 to 90 days, depending on environmental conditions, pest pressure, and the products used. Exterior treatments break down faster due to weather exposure. Interior treatments in protected areas like basements and attics last longer. Quarterly service schedules align with seasonal pest cycles and maintain continuous protection throughout the year.

Ready to Take Back Your Home from Spiders?

You shouldn't have to worry about venomous spiders in your living spaces or wonder whether that web in the corner is harmless or a sign of something worse.
